narrative:
The model estimated a 50.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only a slight lean toward failure, but it was enough for the law school to reject your application. The denial should not be read as a certainty that you cannot pass; it reflects a risk estimate based on the information available.

The most influential factor was your third-year class standing. Your decile of 5 was the strongest single signal and, in this assessment, actually leaned toward likely bar success; it was somewhat stronger than the accepted-student average of about 5.8. The second most important factor was your law school admission test score. At 30.5, it was well below the accepted-student average of about 37.2, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. The third factor was your undergraduate grade point average. At 3.0, it was below the accepted-student average of about 3.23 and also pushed toward failure. Together, the test score and undergraduate record outweighed the favorable third-year standing enough to produce the slight failure lean.

To move forward, ask admissions whether the decision can be reconsidered or whether you can submit additional evidence. Consider retaking the admission test after preparation, strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a graduate program, and obtaining letters or statements that address your readiness. Apply to programs with holistic review, and do not treat this prediction as a final judgment of your ability to succeed.
